newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Sri Lanka expands airport for passengers, cargo.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sri Lanka expands airport for passengers, cargo.

text.p: Sri Lanka plans to expand its international airport at Katunayake to cater to growing passenger and cargo traffic, the chairman of the Airport and Aviation Services said.

The $150 million expansion plan includes new passenger and cargo terminals, a new aircraft parking apron and better air traffic control facilities, Captain Sudharshan Manamperi told Reuters in an interview.

The new airport will have several airbridges -- instead of the current system of using buses to ferry passengers to and from aircraft -- and a new domestic terminal. For the first time the airport will have separate international and domestic facilities.
"The new airport will be designed to meet traffic demand by 2010 which we forecast at eight million passengers a year," Manamperi said.
The existing airport, built in the 1980s, was designed for 3.4 million passengers a year, he said. The airport now handles about 2.3 million passengers annually, flown in and out by 28 airlines.
Passenger traffic was growing about eight to nine percent a year, Manamperi said.
Sri Lanka's location makes it ideal for the Indian Ocean island to tap the huge flow of cargo between Europe and the fast-growing Asian region, Manamperi said.

Aviation industry analysts said Sri Lanka could exploit in the air cargo field the reputation of its main Colombo port as a regional container transshipment hub, sitting astride a major East-West shipping route.
Around 30 to 35 percent of world trade by value goes by air, with about 25 percent of manufactured goods by value being carried as air freight.

Manamperi said plans to modernise Bandaranaike International Airport at Katunayake, on the southwest coast 30 km (19 miles) north of Colombo, will raise cargo capacity to 375,000 tonnes a year. In 1995 it handled 76,000 tonnes of cargo.

AirLanka, Sri Lanka's national airline, has said it will create separate import and export cargo complexes by the end of the year 2000 and target shippers throughout the Indian sub-continent to develop Colombo as a regional sea-air hub.

AirLanka cargo sales have increased to almost 15 percent of total group revenues from 9 percent in 1989, following the addition of three Airbus Industrie A340s over the past two years, airline officials said.
The plan is for freight to converge at Colombo's sea container port and then be shipped by air to long-haul destinations in Europe, the United States and the Far East, they said.
Transshipment now accounts for 30 percent of all freight carried on Airlanka, with the balance mainly local import-export traffic.

Manamperi also said that as part of its expansion, the airport will upgrade its air traffic control facilities with the construction of a Secondary Surveillance monopulse radar that will allow controllers better control of aircraft.
New air traffic control concepts will also be adopted to handle a bigger volume of aircraft through the Colombo Flight Information Region, which now deals with about 500 aircraft a month, he said.
